title: Question 9
stem:
A rigid copper wire is held horizontally between the pole pieces of two magnets, as shown in Fig. 9.1.

{{figure:figure_9_1}}

The width of each pole piece is $8.5\text{ cm}$.
The uniform magnetic flux density $B$ in the region between the poles of the magnets is $3.7\text{ mT}$ and is zero outside this region.
The angle between the wire and the direction of the magnetic field is $\theta$.
The current in the wire is in the direction shown on Fig. 9.1.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: By reference to the **side** view of Fig. 9.1, state and explain the direction of the force on the **magnets**.

markscheme_points.text: using Fleming's left-hand rule force on wire
by Newton's third law, force on magnet is opposite

hints: Hint 1: Look carefully at the side view - which way is the current pointing and which way does the magnetic field go from the N-pole to the S-pole between the magnets?
Hint 2: First work out which way the field pushes the wire, then remember the wire must push back equally on whatever is producing the field.
parts.proper_answer: Force on magnets is vertically downwards. Fleming's left-hand rule gives force on wire vertically upwards, so by Newton's third law the force on the magnets is equal and opposite.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the force on the wire**
Picture yourself sitting beside the side view. The current $I$ is to the right. The magnetic field $B$ goes from N to S, which here is into the plane of the side view. Using Fleming's left-hand rule with First finger along $B$ and second finger along $I$, your thumb points upwards. So the magnetic force on the wire is vertically upwards.

Step 2: **Use Newton to get the force on the magnets**
A magnetic force is an interaction between the wire and the magnets. If the magnets push up on the wire, the wire pushes down on the magnets. By Newton's third law the forces are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction. Hence the force on the magnets is vertically downwards.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem: The constant current in the wire is $5.1\text{ A}$.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: For angle $\theta$ equal to $90^{\circ}$, calculate the force on the wire.
hints: Hint 1: For $\theta = 90^{\circ}$ the wire is at right angles to the field, so the full width of the pole pieces is effective. Check what $B$, $I$ and that length are in SI units.
Hint 2: Combine $B$, $I$ and $L$ for the perpendicular case to get the magnitude, remembering $1\text{ mT} = 10^{-3}\text{ T}$ and $8.5\text{ cm} = 8.5\times 10^{-2}\text{ m}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Identify the governing law**
When current is perpendicular to a uniform field, the magnetic force is largest and given by $$F = BIL$$ where $L$ is the length of wire actually inside the field. Here $B = 3.7\text{ mT} = 3.7\times 10^{-3}\text{ T}$, $I = 5.1\text{ A}$ and $L = 8.5\text{ cm} = 8.5\times 10^{-2}\text{ m}$.

Step 2: **Substitute and calculate**
$$F = (3.7\times 10^{-3}) \times 5.1 \times (8.5\times 10^{-2})$$ $$F \approx 1.6\times 10^{-3}\text{ N}$$ This is the force on the wire, directed upwards as in (a).

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text:
The angle $\theta$ is changed to $60^{\circ}$.
The length of wire in the magnetic field is $\left(\dfrac{8.5}{\sin 60^{\circ}}\right)\text{ cm}$.
Calculate the force on the wire.
hints: Hint 1: At $60^{\circ}$ the wire cuts the field obliquely, so the length in the field gets longer but only the perpendicular component counts - think how those two effects combine.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **See why the angle cancels out**
The general form is $$F = BIL\sin\theta$$ where $L$ is now the longer slanted length in the field, $$L = \frac{8.5\times 10^{-2}}{\sin 60^{\circ}}\text{ m}$$ So $$F = BI\left(\frac{8.5\times 10^{-2}}{\sin 60^{\circ}}\right)\sin 60^{\circ} = BI\times 8.5\times 10^{-2}$$ The $\sin 60^{\circ}$ cancels. Numerically this is exactly the (b)(i) calculation, $$F = 1.6\times 10^{-3}\text{ N}$$ A longer length is exactly compensated by the smaller perpendicular component.

key_concepts: component of length perpendicular to field

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
The constant current in the wire is now changed to an alternating current of frequency $20\text{ Hz}$ and root-mean-square (r.m.s.) value $5.1\text{ A}$.

The angle between the wire and the direction of the magnetic field is $90^{\circ}$.

On Fig. 9.2, sketch a graph to show the variation with time $t$ of the force $F$ on the wire for two cycles of the alternating current.

{{figure:figure_9_2}}

markscheme_points.text: sketch: sinusoidal wave with two cycles

hints: Hint 1: Since $F$ is directly proportional to $I$ at $90^{\circ}$, what shape must the $F$-$t$ graph have if $I$-$t$ is sinusoidal, and what is its frequency?
Hint 2: Work out the time for one cycle from the given $20\text{ Hz}$ frequency, then double it for two cycles.
Hint 3: Remember the $5.1\text{ A}$ given is r.m.s., not peak - how do you convert the $1.6\times 10^{-3}\text{ N}$ r.m.s. force to a peak value for the amplitude of the sketch?
parts.proper_answer: Sinusoidal $F$-$t$ graph through origin, two full cycles, period $0.050\text{ s}$, peak amplitude $2.3\times 10^{-3}\text{ N}$ (positive and negative).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Shape and period**
With $\theta = 90^{\circ}$, $F = BIL$ at every instant, so $F$ follows $I$ exactly. An alternating current gives a sinusoidal $F$, alternating in direction, with the same frequency $f = 20\text{ Hz}$. Period is $$T = \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{20} = 0.050\text{ s}$$ Two cycles therefore last $0.10\text{ s}$. Start at $F=0$ at $t=0$ and draw two complete sine waves.

Step 2: **Amplitude from r.m.s. to peak**
The calculated $1.6\times 10^{-3}\text{ N}$ corresponds to the r.m.s. current $5.1\text{ A}$. For a sine wave, $$\text{peak value} = \sqrt{2} \times \text{r.m.s. value}$$ So $$F_{0} = \sqrt{2}\times 1.6\times 10^{-3} \approx 2.3\times 10^{-3}\text{ N}$$ This is the maximum positive and negative displacement on the $F$-axis.

Step 3: **Complete sketch**
Draw $F/\text{N}$ vertical versus $t/\text{s}$ horizontal, with a sine curve centred on $F=0$, amplitude $2.3\times 10^{-3}\text{ N}$, crossing zero every $0.025\text{ s}$ and repeating every $0.050\text{ s}$ for two cycles.
